title: Trilochan: the last thought
hook: what we think of at the very end shapes where we go (Gujri, Trilochan, ang 526)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhagat: a leather-worker's songs, kept by Sikhs and by the Ravidassia, a song for all. Today, a new Bhagat, and a hard question.

What was on your mind just before you fell asleep last night? A bill. A message you shouldn't have sent. Tomorrow's meeting. A face. Sometimes that thought is still there in the morning. Trilochan's hymn is about that last thought, stretched to its limit: not the last thought before sleep, but the last one at the very end of a life.
screen: `THE THOUGHT BEFORE SLEEP.` → `STILL THERE IN THE MORNING.` → `TRILOCHAN: THE VERY END.`

segments.voice: Trilochan is one of the devotees Ravidas named three days ago, and today he gets his own hymn, in Raag Gujri, on Ang 526 of the Guru Granth Sahib. Its refrain, the line it keeps coming back to, is a plea to a sister, in paraphrase: O sister, don't forget the Name of Gobind. Then he builds a ladder of pictures, each in the same frame. At the last moment, whoever thinks of wealth, and dies in that thought, is born again and again as a serpent, coiled around the treasure, you might say. Whoever thinks of sons and family is born as a pig, nosing among a crowd of young. Whoever thinks of mansions dies and wanders like a ghost, haunting the halls. Each picture is the thought made into a body: in the hymn, what a person holds onto at the end, they become. Then the last verse turns. Whoever, at the last moment, thinks of the Lord and dies in that thought is set free, and the Lord, the hymn says, dwells in that heart. It's a warning. Many readers also hear something practical in it: the thought that shows up at the end is likely the one that's been showing up all along, at red lights, in the shower, at two in the morning. That's why the refrain isn't about dying. It's about not forgetting, today. In the Sikh telling, the Name is remembered through simran, steady remembrance. The pictures are strange, even a little grim, but the plea underneath is gentle: sister, don't forget.
screen: `O SISTER, DON'T FORGET THE NAME.` · `WEALTH, FAMILY, MANSIONS: THE THOUGHT BECOMES A BODY.` · `THE LORD AT THE END: SET FREE.` · then, large: `THE LAST THOUGHT IS PRACTICED NOW.`

segments.voice: Choose a good thought to end today with, while it's easy: a face you love, a line from this path, a moment you're grateful for, or, if you pray, the Name. Say it to yourself slowly, until it's short enough to find in the dark. Then rest with it, breathing out Waheguru if that's yours.
Trilochan. The Bhagat of Raag Gujri whose refrain is a plea to a sister: don't forget the Name, because the last thought is made of all the others.
Your line: the last thought. It's being practiced right now. Day seven hundred eighty, done.

screen: `DAY 780 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BENI: THE STAGES OF LIFE.`

howItsDone: Trilochan's hymn is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs traditionally end the day with Kirtan Sohila, the bedtime prayer, and simran, remembering the Name before sleep.

chat.says: What's Trilochan's hymn about? I heard it mentions snakes and ghosts.
options: The last thought: what you dwell on at the end, you become, so don't forget the Name now.
It's a ghost story warning people to stay away from old houses and mansions.
It says only deathbed prayers matter, so the rest of life can wait.
chat.meaning: In Raag Gujri, Trilochan pictures each last thought becoming a body, and his refrain asks: sister, don't forget the Name of Gobind.

notes: Hymn paraphrased from memory (refrain: are baaee gobid naam mat beesrai). Confirm the verse images: wealth/serpent, sons/pig, mansions/ghost (pret), the Lord/liberation.
